Remember one principle: File Clerks file accurately, retrieve quickly, and control access strictly. They must always explain where each document is.

It is a poor fit for careless, highly active, or overly talkative people. Records rooms are quiet and enclosed, with daily sorting and cataloging. Restless or inattentive workers can create problems quickly.

A common path is: study secretarial work or records management, or enter through administration; learn classification and file creation; learn digitization tools; gain a professional records credential or study information science; then move into records supervision or data governance.

This occupation suits careful, organized people who can sit for long periods and protect confidential information. Filing has little tolerance for error. A misplaced or unregistered file can cause serious problems, and the work requires comfort with quiet, repetitive tasks.

File Clerks receive, register, classify, file, scan, retrieve, and manage the lending of documents. They protect record integrity and confidentiality and keep information organized and searchable across paper and electronic systems.

paragraphs: The daily rhythm is receive, file, and retrieve. File Clerks register, number, scan, and archive new documents, then process loan requests by searching catalogs, retrieving files, and recording access. Quarterly audits can require days of reviewing evidence, completing catalogs, and transferring records. Highly digital organizations focus more on metadata and filing rules than paper.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 84,300 File Clerks were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 70,900 by 2034, a net decrease of about 13,400 jobs, with about 7,300 openings each year. The median annual wage was about $41,300 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will substantially reduce the number of File Clerks. Automated scanning, intelligent classification, and semantic search already handle much filing and retrieval, and paper-only roles are shrinking quickly. Records appraisal, confidentiality levels, destruction approval, and complex retrieval still require people who understand policy and accept responsibility. The occupation is shifting toward records management and data governance.

paragraphs: A score of 7/10 indicates moderate-high AI exposure in this administrative occupation. AI excels at scanning, classification, and retrieval, creating high replacement risk for operational roles. Policy management, confidentiality, and complex retrieval still require people.

Moderate-high exposure requires active transition. Stop investing only in manual filing skills that systems can replace. Move toward records management, data governance, and information security. Using AI as a tool can shift the role from operator to administrator.

Students interested in administrative work can study records management, but should also learn confidentiality law, data management, and digital archives. Digital-records roles offer stronger prospects than traditional clerical work.
Learn digital archives platforms and AI search tools. Pursue professional records credentials or further study in information science. Moving from paper to data can improve both role level and pay.

Clerical workers can transition into records roles by learning records law, electronic-records management, and confidentiality systems. In interviews, explain the complete lifecycle of a document and emphasize organization and responsibility.
